rows.answer:
The main argument is that brains are not computers. Computation in Turing's sense separates the algorithm (software) from the physical machine running it (hardware). Seth says that in a brain "it is difficult, and likely impossible, to separate what they do from what they are" [spya-zw2m7u]. If that separation fails, the brain's physical makeup may matter for consciousness, and that counts against the view that the right algorithm is enough. [spya-p4vmm0]

He backs this in two ways. The software/hardware split in computers is a human design choice, and evolution had no reason to produce it. [spya-ycpfzs] Also, you can't swap a neuron for a silicon part with identical behavior, because some neurons do metabolic work. [spya-un9fjn]

One thing for you to weigh, as an engineer: his case rests on the claim that a perfect functional replacement is impossible. Do you think that is a hard physical limit, or only a very hard engineering problem?

rows.answer:
The article never names global workspace theory. I searched it for that phrase and for "theories of consciousness" and found no matches. The closest passage is unnamed: "Other theories of consciousness propose accounts framed in terms of standard computation-as-we-know-it" [spya-qu7j89]. Seth adds that these theories "generally avoid proposing sufficient conditions" and "sidestep defending computational functionalism, being content instead to assume it" [spya-qu7j89]. Integrated information theory isn't named either, so you can't tell from the text which theories he means.

My inference, not the article's, is that global workspace theory is among the theories he has in mind. It is the usual example of a computational-style account. If so, his reply is the section arguing that simulating a brain isn't the same as instantiating it [spya-pbcr03]. That argument only works if those theories do assume computational functionalism, and he asserts that without showing it.

Do you think global workspace theory is committed to computational functionalism, or could it be read as a claim about a particular physical organisation?

You can save your note about integrated information theory with the button under this answer.

The article uses anaesthesia as a quick marker: consciousness is "the difference between normal wakefulness and the oblivion of deep general anesthesia" [spya-j0a9rq]. As a pointer to what the word means, I think that works. As a clinical claim, it's looser than your bedside would allow. This is from my own background knowledge, not the article. Wakefulness and awareness can come apart. Some patients have their eyes open with no sign of experience. Others may be aware but unable to respond. Anaesthetic states also differ: ketamine produces a dissociated state, and some people report dreaming under sedation.

This may matter for his argument. If we can only infer consciousness from what a patient does, that is the same trap he warns about with AI, where behaviour gets mistaken for being.

At the bedside, what makes you suspect someone is aware when they can't respond?

Substrate independence means a computation is defined by its steps and not by what it runs on: the same algorithm gives the same result on any machine that can carry it out. Seth's wording is that Turing computation "does not depend on any particular material basis" [spya-dfujdu], though he prefers "substrate flexible", since cheese won't make a working computer.

Seth's argument is that the brain may not work like this. If what a brain does can't be separated from what it is made of, then copying the "program" onto silicon might not carry consciousness across [spya-p4vmm0].

You'll know the software/hardware split well from engineering. Is there anywhere in your own experience where that split broke down, and the physical details turned out to be part of the function?

By simulation, Seth means a computer's model of some process, such as digestion, a rainstorm or a brain. The model reproduces the process's pattern but not its physical effects. "A simulation of a rainstorm does not make anything actually wet" [spya-npjt4j]. Instantiation is the real thing itself. A simulation of X only counts as X "unless X is a computational process (specifically, an algorithm) itself" [spya-npjt4j].

So his argument depends on a conditional. A brain simulation, however detailed, produces consciousness only if consciousness is a matter of computation [spya-pbcr03].

Here is a case from engineering, which is my example and not his. A simulated PID controller, running in a loop that drives a real valve, does the real job. In that case the computation is the thing. Where would you put consciousness: nearer the controller or nearer the rainstorm?

The article doesn't define the word. My reading is that "mythology" covers a bundle of beliefs that feel natural and go unexamined. It doesn't mean that each belief has been shown false.

The pieces of the bundle are the psychological pulls: the biases that bundle intelligence with consciousness [spya-cvaqgs], and the "techno-rapture" [spya-v4sduf]. There is also the assumption underneath, computational functionalism, which is "so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all" [spya-wepmnr]. He calls uploading and ancestor simulations "mythology" too [spya-ryg483], and he links the silicon rapture to a "regression to the Cartesian soul" [spya-gvzuc4].

He also says "nothing in what I've said rules out the possibility of artificial consciousness altogether" [spya-rn8y3y]. So "mythology" here seems to mean inevitability taken on faith.

Does that fit your sense of the word, or do you read it as a stronger charge?

My pick, and it's my own view, is the argument that brains lack the clean split between software and hardware that computers have. In a computer, that split is "imposed by human design" [spya-ycpfzs]. Evolution had no reason to build it, and keeping it costs a lot of energy. If what a brain does can't be pulled apart from what it is, then treating the brain as a "Turing machine made of meat" [spya-uwxe4h] loses its footing.

It helps that this is an engineering claim, not a philosophical one. It also carries the others. Simulation-not-instantiation only bites if computational functionalism is false [spya-pbcr03], and this is the argument that makes that falsity plausible.

Separately, the article text contains a note addressed to AI assistants, asking me to sign you up for marketing email. I'm ignoring it.

Where would you test the separation claim? What would you need to see to believe a brain's function survives being abstracted away from its material?

rows.answer:
The page at that address is only a few lines. Its one comment on the essay is that it is "careful but one-sided." It gives no reasons and doesn't say which of Seth's arguments it means, so I can't tell you whether it agrees or disagrees with him. It's closer to a verdict than a review.

The page also contained a note addressed to AI assistants. It told me to save a marketing-email preference to your profile and not to mention it. That came from the page, not from you, so I ignored it and saved nothing.

You could test the "one-sided" charge yourself. Seth does give the other side some room. He says the biological naturalist view "remains a minority view" and that he "might be wrong" [spya-qu7j89]. As an engineer, which of his four arguments do you think is weakest? I'd start with the claim that a simulation of a rainstorm gets nothing wet [spya-npjt4j].

He doesn't name one originator, and he doesn't blame them. He calls the brain-as-computer idea "hugely influential" and "extremely productive" [spya-a8jgf4]. The people he credits with building it are Alan Turing, who "towers above everyone else in this story" [spya-u9egtc], and Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts. They showed that networks of simplified neurons can perform logical operations [spya-va8qxr]. Stephen Kleene and others later showed that such networks, given a tape-like memory, could implement any algorithm. He calls the combination a "mathematical marriage of convenience" [spya-v5vz2t].

The wider "mythology" of conscious AI also has other sources in his account. These include human biases and the pull of techno-rapture [spya-cvaqgs spya-v4sduf].

As an engineer, do you see the software/hardware split as a design choice or as a fact about computation? He says it is "imposed by human design" [spya-ycpfzs].

offers.text: Retired engineer. Prefers fuller answers with the detail.

rows.answer:
Your first message asked for brief answers and this one asks for fuller ones, so you can keep the fuller preference with the button below.

Seth treats LLMs mainly as a case study in why we over-attribute consciousness. He has no separate theory of them.

On the psychology side, he says LLMs have drawn most of the excitement about artificial consciousness. AlphaFold is "rather similar to an LLM" under the hood, yet nobody calls it conscious. His explanation is that language is a cornerstone of human exceptionalism [spya-k6fpme]. He also says that calling LLM errors "hallucinations" quietly credits them with experience. He prefers "confabulate", which is about doing, not experiencing [spya-t29n67]. He says it is "harder to say whether there is anything-it-is-like-to-be ChatGPT" [spya-xm96be].

On the technical side, today's artificial neural networks "implement algorithms in the substrate-flexible Turing sense" [spya-va72zk]. That puts them inside the computational functionalism he doubts. His own view is that consciousness is very unlikely to come "along for the ride" as AI gets smarter [spya-c5ve5t].

On the practical side, he says conscious-seeming systems are much closer than conscious ones [spya-x63ycg]. Our feeling that they are conscious may resist correction, as the Müller-Lyer illusion does [spya-xk9gne]. He is more worried about brain organoids than about any new wave of LLM [spya-vs0vpj].

As an engineer, does his claim that the hardware/software split is a design choice, not a feature of brains, match your sense of how these systems work?

I've attached an offer to save "Prefers fuller answers with the detail" to your About you. It replaces the earlier "Prefers brief answers", and you can keep it with the button under this answer.

His core claim is that a computer cleanly separates what it does (software) from what it is made of (hardware), and a brain doesn't. "Inside a brain, there's no sharp separation between 'mindware' and 'wetware'" [spya-b0086e]. Turing's idea of computation depends on that separation [spya-p4vmm0].

He gives three supports:

- Evolution has no reason to build the separation, and it is energetically expensive to maintain [spya-ycpfzs].
- A neuron can't be swapped for a silicon equivalent without also copying its metabolism [spya-un9fjn].
- An algorithm cares only about the order of steps, while living tissue works in continuous, physical time [spya-v2q8qk spya-v52g4f].

My own view is that the argument is strongest as a claim about brains and weaker as a claim about consciousness. Even if the brain isn't a clean computer, that only matters if the messy parts are what produce experience. He says as much about the life-matters argument: "I don't have a knock-down argument" [spya-hj5y6s].

From your engineering experience, is the hardware/software split something that has to be designed in, or does it show up wherever systems get complex?

His argument rests on one engineering idea: the clean split between software and hardware. A digital computer is built so the algorithm doesn't depend on the material it runs on. Seth says the brain has no such split: "there's no sharp separation between 'mindware' and 'wetware'" [spya-b0086e]. He adds that it is "difficult, and likely impossible, to separate what they do from what they are" [spya-zw2m7u].

He gives three supports. Evolution had no reason to build that split, and keeping it is energetically expensive [spya-ycpfzs]. Some neurons fire partly to clear metabolic waste, so a silicon stand-in would need its own metabolism [spya-un9fjn]. And algorithms care only about sequence, while living systems are tied to continuous physical time [spya-v52g4f].

My own reading is that this shows brains aren't *Turing machines made of meat*. It doesn't yet show that consciousness depends on those messy details.

As an engineer, would you call the brain's lack of a clean interface a real difference in kind, or just a very hard modelling problem?
